text: To postulate something is to put it forward as true, or as existing, so you can reason from it before you have proof. Pauli proposed an invisible particle in 1930 to explain energy that seemed to go missing in a kind of radioactive decay, then worried that no instrument could ever catch it. As a noun, a postulate is a starting assumption, like the postulates of geometry.

An elucidation is the work of making something clear that was murky before; the root is the Latin for light, as in lucid. Here it means the decades physicists spent working out what neutrinos are actually like after they were first detected in 1956, work that earned several Nobel prizes. It is a formal word, found more in textbooks and reviews than in conversation.

Diminutive means strikingly small. In grammar a diminutive is also a word ending that marks something as little, and the article plays on both senses: the Italian ending -ino means little, so neutrino means roughly little neutral one, a name that announces exactly why the particle is so hard to catch.

Wolfgang Pauli was an Austrian physicist and one of the founders of quantum mechanics, who won the Nobel prize in physics in 1945. In 1930 he proposed the neutrino to explain missing energy in radioactive decay, and was uneasy about suggesting something he thought could never be detected.

A theoretical physicist works out the laws of nature with mathematics and reasoning rather than by running experiments. The split matters in this story: Pauli the theorist predicted the neutrino in 1930, and experimenters needed another 26 years to build equipment that could actually detect one.

A neutrino is a fundamental particle, meaning it is not made of anything smaller, with no electric charge and an extremely tiny mass. Because it interacts with ordinary matter only through the weak nuclear force, nearly every neutrino passes straight through people, buildings and the whole Earth without touching anything, which is what makes it so hard to detect.

A subatomic particle is anything smaller than an atom: the protons, neutrons and electrons that atoms are made of, and more exotic ones like the neutrino. Sub- means below, so the word literally means below the level of the atom.

Peculiar means strange or unusual, and it can also mean belonging especially to one thing, as in a habit peculiar to cats. Both senses fit here: the neutrino's properties were odd, and they were particular to this one kind of particle, which is why no device of the 1930s could catch it.

To fox someone is British slang for baffling or outwitting them, like a clever fox. Saying the neutrino would have foxed any contemporary device means no detector of the time could have coped with it. It has nothing to do with being attractive, the American slang sense of foxy.

Contemporary usually means modern, as in contemporary art, but its older and more exact meaning is existing at the same time as something else. That is the sense here: any contemporary device means any device that existed back in 1930, not a modern one. It is a common trap in reading history.

A string of means a series of similar things coming one after another, like beads on a string. A string of Nobel prizes means several prizes over the years, each for a further discovery about neutrinos, not just one.

Francis Halzen is a Belgian-born physicist at the University of Wisconsin-Madison who won the 2026 Nobel prize in physics. Starting in 1988 he pushed the idea of using deep Antarctic ice as a giant neutrino detector, which became the IceCube Observatory.

Astrophysical describes anything to do with the physics of stars, galaxies and other objects in space. Astrophysical sources here are the unknown objects far out in the universe that produce extremely energetic particles, as opposed to sources on or near Earth.

A light-year is a distance, not a length of time: how far light travels in one year, about 9.5 trillion kilometres. Sources light-years from Earth are far beyond our solar system; even the nearest star is more than four light-years away.

Elusive means hard to find, catch or pin down. Neutrinos are elusive not because they hide but because they almost never interact with the matter that detectors are made of, so they slip through unnoticed.

Something electrically neutral has no overall electric charge, neither positive nor negative. That matters because the electromagnetic force, which holds atoms together and stops your hand going through a desk, only acts on charged things, so a neutral particle feels none of it.

Hence means for this reason, or that is why. In the article it points at the source of each half of the name: neutral, hence the neutr-; tiny, hence the -ino. It is formal and common in science and argument writing.

To render something a certain way is to make it become that way, as in the news rendered her speechless. Here, the neutrino's lack of charge and tiny size render it, meaning make it, effectively immune to electromagnetism and gravity. It has nothing to do with rendering graphics or art.

In effect means in practice, even if not strictly or technically. The writer uses it carefully: gravity does technically pull on neutrinos, but their mass is so tiny the pull makes no practical difference, so in effect they are immune.

Immune most often means protected from a disease, but its broader meaning is not affected by something at all. Here neutrinos are immune to the electromagnetic force and gravity in the sense that those forces have practically no effect on them.

The electromagnetic force acts between electrically charged particles, pulling opposite charges together and pushing like charges apart. It holds electrons to atoms and atoms to each other, and it is behind electricity, magnetism and light. It is one of the four fundamental forces of physics.

The weak nuclear force is one of the four fundamental forces of physics. It causes some kinds of radioactive decay and drives part of the fusion that powers the Sun, but it only acts over distances smaller than an atomic nucleus. It is the main way a neutrino can affect anything, which is why neutrinos so rarely do.

Feeble means weak, lacking strength or force, and it can describe a body, an effort or an excuse. The weak nuclear force is feeble enough that almost every neutrino passes through matter without being stopped.

Abundant means existing in large quantities, more than plenty. Neutrinos are abundant throughout the universe: tens of billions from the Sun alone pass through every fingernail-sized patch of your skin each second.

A by-product is something produced along the way while making something else, often not the thing anyone wanted. Neutrinos are a by-product of nuclear reactions: the reactions release energy, and neutrinos stream out as a side effect.

Nuclear fission is the splitting of a heavy atomic nucleus, such as uranium, into smaller pieces, which releases a great deal of energy. It powers nuclear power stations, and it gives off neutrinos as a side effect.

Nuclear fusion is the joining of light atomic nuclei, such as hydrogen, into heavier ones, which releases enormous energy. It is what powers the Sun and every other star, and the reactions throw off vast numbers of neutrinos.

A proton is a positively charged particle found in the nucleus of every atom. The protons in this story are flying through space on their own at enormous speeds; because they carry charge, magnetic fields bend their paths on the way to Earth.

A particle accelerator is a machine that uses electric and magnetic fields to speed particles up to enormous energies, like the Large Hadron Collider near Geneva. Calling the unknown cosmic sources natural particle accelerators means something out in space does the same job, only far more powerfully.

To be deflected is to be knocked off a straight course and sent in a different direction, as a goalkeeper deflects a shot. Charged protons are deflected by magnetic fields in space, so the direction they arrive from no longer points back to where they started.

Perchloroethylene is a chemical used as dry-cleaning fluid. Early neutrino experiments filled giant tanks with it because it is cheap and full of chlorine atoms, which, very rarely, a passing neutrino turns into a detectable atom of argon.

A vat is a large tank or tub for holding liquid, the kind used in breweries or factories. The early neutrino detectors were enormous vats of fluid, so big because a neutrino interaction is so rare that you need a huge number of atoms to catch even one.

Constituent means forming part of a whole. The fluid's constituent atoms are the atoms it is made of. As a noun, a constituent is also a voter in a politician's district, a different but related sense: one of the people who make up the electorate.

Extrasolar means coming from outside our solar system. Extra- means outside, as in extraordinary, and solar refers to the Sun. Extrasolar neutrinos come from distant cosmic sources rather than from the Sun, and they are far rarer.

The Nobel Committee for Physics is the panel of Swedish scientists that recommends who should win the physics prize each year. Its secretary explained this year's choice, including why the prize went to Halzen alone.

Blue Peter is a long-running British television show for children, famous since 1958 for hands-on demonstrations and craft projects. Saying the committee's explanation was worthy of Blue Peter means it was a simple, homemade-style demonstration.

A repository is a place where a large amount of something is stored, like a library for books or a database for code; programmers know the word from code repositories. Earth's vast repositories of ice are its huge natural stores, chiefly the Antarctic ice sheet, which is up to several kilometres thick.

The IceCube Observatory is a neutrino detector at the South Pole: 5,160 light sensors lowered on cables into holes melted deep into the Antarctic ice, filling about a cubic kilometre. It was completed in 2011 and is run by around 450 researchers in 14 countries.

Atomic nuclei is the plural of atomic nucleus, the tiny, dense centre of an atom made of protons and neutrons. When a neutrino does hit a nucleus in the ice, the collision produces a fast charged particle that gives off a faint flash of blue light, which IceCube's sensors record.

Radiation means energy given off as waves or particles, and it does not always mean something dangerous: light is radiation. Here it means the faint flashes of light produced in the ice when a neutrino collision sends a charged particle racing through it.

To bear fruit means to produce good results, the way a tree eventually produces fruit after years of growing. IceCube bore fruit quickly: two years after it was finished, it detected the first high-energy neutrinos from space.
The cosmos is the universe seen as an ordered whole. The word comes from Greek for order, and it is also the root of cosmic. A new window onto the cosmos means a new way of observing the universe.

A window onto something is a way of seeing it that was not available before. Opening a new window onto the cosmos means neutrinos let astronomers observe the universe in a way that light-based telescopes cannot.

A quirk is an odd, slightly surprising feature or habit. One of the Nobel foundation's quirks is its rule capping each prize at three winners, which fits awkwardly with modern science, where big discoveries often come from teams of hundreds.
Statutes are formal written rules or laws. The Nobel foundation's statutes are the rulebook that governs how the prizes work, including the limit of three winners per prize.

A collaboration is people working together on something. In science, a collaboration is also the formal name for a big multinational research team, like the hundreds of scientists who build and run IceCube together.

Vision here does not mean eyesight: it means the ability to imagine what could be done and plan for it before anyone else does. The committee credits Halzen's scientific vision because he pictured a detector made of Antarctic ice years before it was built.
